Revisiting meta-analytic estimates of validity in personnel selection: Addressing systematic overcorrection for restriction of range. Journal of Applied Psychology, 107(11), 2040-2068. https://doi.org/10.1037/apl0000994 (advance online publication 2021). exact_quotes: Abstract (p.1): "we conclude that each has significant issues that often result in substantial overcorrection and that therefore the validity of many selection procedures for predicting job performance has been substantially overestimated."

Abstract (p.1): "Key findings are that most of the same selection procedures that ranked high in prior summaries remain high in rank, but with mean validity estimates reduced by .10-.20 points. Structured interviews emerged as the top-ranked selection procedure."
Abstract (p.1): "We conclude that our selection procedures remain useful, but selection predictor-criterion relationships are considerably lower than previously thought."
Introduction (p.1): "We acknowledge that we ourselves have errantly drawn upon these approaches in our research, cited them in past studies, and taught them to our students."

Approach 1 section (p.3-4): "The takeaway message is that applying a correction factor derived from predictive studies to concurrent studies, where restriction is generally minimal, results in an overestimate of validity."

Approach 1 section: "We offer the proposition that the vast majority of validation research is concurrent. The percent of studies that are concurrent from various meta-analyses include 98% in Roth et al. (2005) work sample meta-analysis, 95% in McDaniel et al.'s (2007) SJT meta-analysis, 76% in Ones et al.'s (1993) integrity test meta-analysis, 74% in Huffcutt et al.'s (2014) interview meta-analysis"
Discussion, Table 3 commentary (p.23): "The mean across Schmidt and Hunter's top five was .49, while the mean across our top five is .37."

Discussion (p.23): "While structured interviews fared well in prior work, they do emerge in the present work as the strongest predictor of job performance. This suggests a reframing: while Schmidt and Hunter (1998) positioned cognitive ability as the focal predictor, with others evaluated in terms of their incremental validity over cognitive ability, one might propose structured interviews as the focal predictor against which others are evaluated."

Discussion (p.23): "We call attention to the fact that the strongest predictors in our re-analysis (structured interviews, job knowledge tests, empirically keyed biodata, and work samples) are all job-specific measures."

Discussion (p.24): "while the structured interview has the highest mean operational validity (.42), it also has a large residual SD of .19. Thus, while the mean is high, there is also a higher risk of obtaining a lower value."

Discussion, Main Conclusions: "Our predictors are useful; but the predictive relationships are considerably weaker than previously thought. We acknowledge that these are not findings that will be eagerly embraced by the field. We wish we could report better news."

Discussion: "Work Samples. The work sample validity estimate decreased by .21, from .54 to .33. This is the result of a new meta-analysis, with the earlier estimate coming from a study pre-dating the development of meta-analysis."
Discussion: "Cognitive ability. The cognitive ability validity estimate decreased by .20, from .51 to .31."
Discussion: "Unstructured Interviews. The unstructured interview validity estimate decreased by .19, from .38 to .19."
Implications for meta-analysts: "if one is not confident in the basis for a range restriction correction, it is better to forego a correction than to use a value that results in an overestimate."

Closing section: "we do not put a stake in the ground regarding the meta-analytic estimates we put forward here; rather, we eagerly await the availability of the data that will permit further refinement of our estimates."
date_and_recency: Advance online 2021; print issue November 2022 (JAP 107(11)). Re-analyses meta-analyses published from the 1980s to the late 2010s (e.g., Hunter 1983 GATB data, McDaniel et al. 1994, Dye et al. 1993, Roth et al. 2005, Huffcutt et al. 2014). Underlying validation studies span decades and predate AI coding tools entirely; the authors note the databases 'predate this technology revolution' (referring to new measurement technology such as game-based assessments). No AI model versions are involved.
key_claims: The five common ways meta-analysts build range restriction artifact distributions (deriving U from a subset of studies, estimating U from hiring rates, using test publisher norms, assuming a distribution, and related approaches) each have flaws that usually cause substantial overcorrection, so the validity of many selection procedures has been substantially overestimated.

Most validation studies are concurrent (incumbents tested). In concurrent studies range restriction can only be indirect, and indirect restriction only shrinks predictor variance much if the original selection method correlates very highly with the predictor (around .80 or more), which the authors judge implausible since observed predictor intercorrelations top out around .50.

Applying a correction factor derived from predictive (applicant) studies to concurrent studies inflates validity. The dominant flaw found was failure to separate predictive and concurrent studies (21 of the meta-analyses judged inappropriately corrected).

Principle of conservative estimation: absent a credible basis for a range restriction correction, report the validity corrected only for criterion unreliability (using .60 interrater reliability) and call it conservative.
Revised estimates keep a similar ranking to Schmidt and Hunter (1998) but lower magnitudes by roughly .10-.20. Structured interviews become the top-ranked predictor (.42).

The strongest predictors are job-specific measures (structured interviews, job knowledge tests, empirically keyed biodata, work samples), suggesting a closer behavioural match between predictor and criterion helps; 'sample' measures fare well relative to 'sign' measures.
Cognitive ability's validity advantage largely disappears (.31), similar to biodata, integrity tests and personality-based EI, while it keeps much larger Black-White subgroup differences.

Structured interviews have a large residual SD (.19), so results vary a lot across settings; a risk-averse employer might rank by the lower credibility value instead, where biodata, contextualized conscientiousness, job knowledge, work samples and structured interviews lead.

Sensitivity analysis: using .52 criterion reliability adds about .02 on average (max .03); a deliberately generous indirect range restriction correction (rzx = .50, selection ratio .05) adds about .02 on average (max .04).
headline_figures: Structured employment interviews: operational validity rho = .42 (SD rho .19, lower 80% credibility value .18, B-W d .23) vs Schmidt & Hunter (1998) .51. Built from McDaniel et al. (1994) reliability-corrected .37 and Huffcutt et al. (2014) re-corrected .45, sample-size weighted.

Job knowledge tests: .40 (SD .13, lower CV .23, B-W d .54) vs .48 in Schmidt & Hunter. Based on Dye et al. (1993) job-specific tests (59 studies, mean observed r .31, corrected for criterion unreliability only).
Empirically keyed biodata: .38 (SD .09, lower CV .26, B-W d .33) vs .35.
Work sample tests: .33 (SD .09, lower CV .21, B-W d .67) vs .54. Based on Roth et al. (2005): 54 studies, 53 concurrent, mean observed r .26; no range restriction correction.
Cognitive ability (GMA) tests: .31 (SD .14, lower CV .13, B-W d .79) vs .51. N-weighted mean of GATB data, Salgado et al. (2003) and Bertua et al. (2005), corrected for criterion unreliability only.
Integrity tests: .31 (SD .20, lower CV .05, B-W d .10) vs .41.
Assessment centers: .29 vs .37. SJT knowledge and behavioural tendency: .26 each.
Unstructured employment interviews: .19 (SD .16, lower CV -.01, B-W d .32) vs .38.
Conscientiousness overall: .19 vs .31. Job experience (years): .07 vs .18. Interests: .24 vs .10 (an increase).
Mean of top five predictors: .37 now vs .49 in Schmidt & Hunter (1998).
Range restriction correction inflation in McDaniel et al. (1994) interview data: structured .37 to .51 (+38%), unstructured .27 to .38 (+41%). Hunter (1983) GATB cognitive ability: .36 to .51 (+42%).

Share of concurrent studies in source meta-analyses: 98% work samples (Roth et al. 2005), 95% SJTs, 76% integrity, 74% interviews (Huffcutt et al. 2014), 78% and 80-85% cognitive ability (Europe, UK), 80% GATB.

Table 5: for cognitive ability (observed .236, .31 after criterion correction), plausible rzx up to .50 never lifts validity above .34 even at extreme selection ratios; averaging rzx .00-.50 across selection ratios adds about .01.
Of the meta-analyses tabulated: 25 judged inappropriately corrected with data unavailable to fix, 13 uncorrected originally, 7 appropriate, 3 re-corrected by the authors.
sample_and_method: Not a new data collection. A systematic re-analysis of existing meta-analyses of selection procedure validity covering the predictors in Schmidt and Hunter (1998) plus newer ones (about 25 predictors in Table 3). Criterion is mostly supervisor ratings of overall job performance across a broad range of jobs (GATB jobs, petroleum industry, general occupations); not specific to software engineers. For each meta-analysis the authors judged the range restriction correction, re-corrected criterion unreliability with .60 where meta-analysts used .52 from the broader literature, applied range restriction corrections only where credible (e.g., only to predictive studies), and combined meta-analyses by N-weighted means. Black-White d values mainly from Dahlke and Sackett (2017).
what_is_measured: Criterion-related (operational) validity of selection procedures for predicting overall job performance, usually supervisor ratings. Predictors include structured and unstructured interviews, work samples, job knowledge tests, cognitive ability, biodata, integrity, personality, SJTs, assessment centers, interests and experience. Nothing specific to coding, design judgement, agent use or tool fluency; the closest analogues for technical hiring are work samples (a coding exercise), job knowledge tests, and structured interviews (e.g., a structured design conversation).
validity_evidence: This source is itself the validity evidence. Corrected operational validities (criterion-unreliability corrected at .60, range restriction corrected only where credible): structured interviews .42, job knowledge .40, empirically keyed biodata .38, work samples .33, GMA .31, integrity .31, assessment centers .29, SJTs .26, unstructured interviews .19, conscientiousness .19, years of experience .07. Prior Schmidt and Hunter (1998) values for the same: .51, .48, .35, .54, .51, .41, .37, n/a, .38, .31, .18. None are specific to software engineering.
relevance_to_angle: Supports moving away from convergent coding tests as the main filter: work samples (the closest analogue to a live coding exercise) fell from .54 to .33, below structured interviews (.42) and job knowledge tests (.40). Supports a structured design conversation: structured interviews rank first and the authors propose them as the focal predictor. Warns against unstructured 'team fit' chats: unstructured interviews are .19 with a credibility interval reaching below zero, so communication and team-fit assessment needs structure to be worth much. Complicates the angle in two ways: (1) the authors stress job-specific 'sample' measures do best, which could be read as backing realistic job tasks (perhaps including working with an agent) rather than dropping task-based assessment; (2) structured interviews have the widest spread (SD .19), so a poorly built one can do much worse than .42. Also undercuts any argument leaning on GMA or puzzle-style tests as superior (.31).
limitations_stated: Criterion comparability: "An implicit assumption in the field is that the overall criterion of 'supervisor ratings of job performance' reflects the same things across studies." They cite head-to-head studies where assessment centers beat ability (.44 vs .22) despite the reverse in separate meta-analyses, and say these "findings suggest caution in comparing findings across meta-analyses".

Predictive vs concurrent designs may not estimate the same thing (faking, test-taker effort, job experience affecting scores); "our treatment also treats both types of studies as estimates of a common operational validity."
Restriction on the criterion (high performers promoted, low performers dismissed) is not corrected; they argue the effect is "likely to be nonzero" but "very small".
Estimates are provisional: "we do not put a stake in the ground regarding the meta-analytic estimates we put forward here".
Uncorrected values are presented as conservative: some degree of restriction is likely, so true values may be somewhat higher (sensitivity analysis suggests about .02-.04).
Subgroup d values partly come from incumbent or mixed samples, adding uncertainty; only Black-White comparisons were available.
Some predictors need trained or experienced candidates (work samples, knowledge tests) while others do not, so comparisons depend on the hiring scenario.
counter_evidence: Oh, Le & Roth (2023, Journal of Applied Psychology 108(8), 1300-1310), 'Revisiting Sackett et al.'s (2022) rationale behind their recommendation against correcting for range restriction in concurrent validation studies', argue from a re-analysis of Sackett et al.'s Table 5 that the paper substantially understates range restriction in concurrent studies, so the revised validities may be too low [uncertain: from abstract and search summaries, full text not opened]. Sackett et al. replied in the same issue (JAP 108(8), 1311-1315), saying they endorse correction when the data exist and that substantial restriction is uncommon [uncertain: abstract-level only]. The follow-on IOP focal article (Sackett et al., 2023, 'Revisiting the design of selection systems...') drew multiple commentaries, some defending larger corrections [uncertain: not opened]. Separately, the paper's own data cut against a simple 'interviews beat coding tests' reading: structured interviews vary widely across settings (SD .19, lower credibility value .18 vs .21 for work samples), and none of the underlying studies involve software engineering or AI-assisted work.
